clinicalPearls: The development of an aggressive lymphoma, most often diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and less commonly classic Hodgkin lymphoma, arising in a patient with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia or small lymphocytic lymphoma
Suggested clinically by rapid nodal enlargement, new B symptoms, a sharply rising lactate dehydrogenase and often disproportionate growth at one site
Most large-cell transformations are clonally related to the underlying chronic lymphocytic leukaemia and carry a poor prognosis, whereas clonally unrelated cases behave more like de novo lymphoma
PET-CT helps localise the most metabolically active site to direct biopsy, and histological confirmation by biopsy is essential
High-risk molecular features of the original disease, particularly TP53 disruption and NOTCH1 mutation, and prior therapy are associated with transformation
Hodgkin-type transformation is frequently Epstein-Barr virus associated and is treated along Hodgkin lymphoma lines
Management is challenging and includes chemoimmunotherapy, consideration of HSCT in fit responders, and enrolment in trials of novel targeted and cellular therapies
reference.pathophysiology: Richter transformation represents the histological progression of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia or small lymphocytic lymphoma into an aggressive lymphoma. In the majority of large-cell cases the transformed clone is genetically derived from the original leukaemic clone, having acquired additional driver lesions such as TP53 disruption, MYC activation, CDKN2A loss and NOTCH1 mutation that confer a proliferative, chemoresistant phenotype. A minority of large-cell cases and many Hodgkin-type transformations are clonally unrelated and, in the latter, Epstein-Barr virus frequently contributes within the immunosuppressed microenvironment of the underlying disease. The clonal relationship and the accumulated genetic damage largely determine the aggressive behaviour and generally poor response to therapy.
additionalDifferentials: Progression or accelerated phase of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia without transformation
De novo diffuse large B-cell lymphoma unrelated to the leukaemia
Prolymphocytic transformation of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia
Classic Hodgkin lymphoma arising in chronic lymphocytic leukaemia
Therapy-related myeloid neoplasm or second malignancy
Infection causing rapid lymphadenopathy in an immunocompromised patient
additionalInvestigations: PET-CT to identify the most metabolically active node for targeted biopsy
Excisional or core biopsy of the suspicious site for histological confirmation
Immunophenotyping and clonality studies to assess relationship to the underlying clone
Molecular testing for TP53, NOTCH1 and MYC abnormalities
Epstein-Barr virus assessment, particularly for Hodgkin-type transformation
Lactate dehydrogenase, blood counts and staging investigations
redFlags: Rapidly enlarging or asymmetrical lymphadenopathy in a patient with known chronic lymphocytic leukaemia
Steeply rising lactate dehydrogenase with new B symptoms
Localised bulky or extranodal mass causing compressive symptoms
Tumour lysis risk with high tumour burden at treatment initiation
reference.prognosis: Clonally related diffuse large B-cell-type Richter transformation carries a poor prognosis with short survival despite intensive therapy, particularly when TP53 is disrupted; clonally unrelated cases and Hodgkin-type transformation generally fare better, and allogeneic HSCT offers the main prospect of durable remission in eligible responders.
pitfalls: Attributing new symptoms to progressive chronic lymphocytic leukaemia and not biopsying to confirm transformation
Biopsying a low-uptake site rather than the most PET-avid lesion
Failing to assess the clonal relationship, which strongly influences prognosis
Overlooking Hodgkin-type transformation, which requires a different treatment approach
Underestimating the tumour lysis and chemoresistance risk of the transformed clone
references: British Society for Haematology guidance on chronic lymphocytic leukaemia
management: Confirm the diagnosis with a PET-directed excisional or core biopsy of the most metabolically active site before treatment
Treat diffuse large B-cell-type transformation with anthracycline-based immunochemotherapy such as rituximab combined with CHOP
Treat Hodgkin-type transformation along Hodgkin lymphoma lines with an ABVD-type regimen
Consolidate responding, eligible patients with allogeneic or autologous haematopoietic stem cell transplantation
Enrol in clinical trials of novel agents, including targeted therapies, immune-checkpoint inhibitors and CAR T-cell therapy, given generally poor outcomes
Assess TP53, NOTCH1 and MYC status and clonal relationship to the underlying chronic lymphocytic leukaemia for prognosis and treatment planning
Provide supportive care with tumour-lysis prophylaxis, infection prophylaxis and transfusion support, managed by a haemato-oncology multidisciplinary team
